task.goal: Reduce wrong-item handoffs in a four-person craft shop that takes custom orders by phone and at the counter.
hard_constraints: No new software purchase or extra shift; the shop must keep taking same-day orders.
Customers may change orders once; revisions must not silently overwrite earlier instructions.
Measure mismatch, added service time and correction burden over two weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing paper tickets, receipt printer and two staff check-ins daily.
task.expected_result: A traceable order handoff design with a failure path.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Numbered order packet with a release gate
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make the paper packet the authoritative record and require a ticket-to-item comparison before release. Give every order a unique handwritten number. Record customer identifier, item, quantity, customization, promised time and distinguishing features; read these back for phone orders and confirm them at the counter. Carry the ticket with the work, and attach its number to the finished item or container. Keep completed orders in numbered locations. The handoff worker compares the customer's identifier, packet number and finished item, including customization, before handing it over.

For the permitted change, retain the original ticket and staple a dated revision marked R1 to its front. Record exactly what changed and who accepted it. Mark the original 'superseded by R1' without obscuring its text. The receiving maker initials R1 before continuing; a revision that arrives during production triggers a physical stop-and-check.

Failure path: missing packet, contradictory instructions, unmatched number or uncertain revision puts that item on hold. Staff locate the record or confirm details with the customer, then document the resolution. Continue accepting same-day orders, quoting feasible completion times while the affected order is resolved.

Needs: paper tickets, pen, staples or clips, space for numbered finished orders and a brief staff walkthrough. Use the two daily check-ins to reconcile unacknowledged revisions and held items. This assumes tickets can stay attached throughout production. It limits record confusion but depends on staff actually inspecting the item; matching numbers alone cannot catch an incorrectly made customization.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over two weeks, alternate comparable half-day blocks between this packet system and current practice, retaining visible revision history in both. Record order volume, wrong-item or wrong-specification releases, mismatches caught before release, added intake and handoff seconds, and correction staff-minutes plus remakes. Review at the existing check-ins. Before launch, stage one revised order and one swapped item: either reaching release undetected falsifies the release gate. Compare mismatch rates and time burden across blocks; low volume or no observed errors leaves effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Independent second-person verification
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: require a second worker to reconstruct what should be handed over from the order record and independently compare it with the finished item. This adds a separate opportunity to detect mistakes that the original maker may overlook. The maker places the finished item with its ticket in a 'needs check' area. Another worker reads the specification directly, checks the actual item, and initials a short paper checklist covering identity, quantity and customization. Only checked items move to the pickup area. At collection, staff match the customer's identifier to that checked packet.

Use a unique number on every ticket. Confirm the recorded specification with the customer when taking the order. Accept one change on a separate dated R1 slip, retaining the original instructions visibly underneath. The maker acknowledges R1. Any change after verification cancels the earlier check and returns the item to 'needs check'; the second worker must inspect it again.

Failure path: disagreement, an unchecked item or an unavailable verifier means no release until another worker verifies or the discrepancy is resolved with the customer. Keep taking same-day orders and explain any affected completion delay. Urgency cannot substitute for the check.

Needs: existing tickets, two labeled areas, and brief checks by another member of the four-person team within current shifts. Use daily check-ins to clear waiting checks and identify repeated discrepancies. The key assumption is sufficient overlap between workers; if one person regularly staffs the shop alone, this design may be impractical. Independence is also fragile if the verifier merely accepts the maker's verbal summary. The added check may become a bottleneck during peaks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate comparable half-day blocks between second-person verification and current practice, using retained revision slips in both. Track eligible orders, checks completed, mismatches caught, mismatches released, added staff-seconds per order, pickup waiting time, and correction minutes and remakes. Include checker time even when the customer does not wait. Stage a wrong customization and a revision received after initial verification; either passing the check exposes a failure. Inspect whether verification coverage falls during busy blocks. Compare against the simpler process without claiming improvement from a small or unbalanced sample.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Customer-confirmed specification at pickup
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use the customer's knowledge of their intended order as the final discrepancy detector. At intake, write a uniquely numbered ticket containing the item, quantity, customization, customer identifier and promised time. Read it back on the phone or show it at the counter. Give counter customers their number and tell phone customers theirs. Keep the ticket with the work until collection.

At pickup, first ask the customer to state the expected item and its key custom feature without prompting from the label. Then show the finished item alongside the recorded specification and ask them to confirm the details before completing the handoff. For wrapped goods, inspect before final wrapping where feasible. Record a brief confirmation mark and the releasing worker's initials. This primarily catches the wrong finished item being selected, while also exposing some production errors.

Accept the single permitted revision on a dated R1 slip attached to the original ticket. Preserve the original wording, mark it superseded, and have the maker acknowledge the new slip. At pickup, explicitly identify the changed feature so an old expectation or overlooked revision becomes visible.

Failure path: disagreement or uncertainty stops release of that item. Compare both instruction versions, contact the ordering customer if needed, document the agreed resolution and arrange correction. Continue taking same-day orders. For a proxy collector, use the ordering customer's confirmation by phone if the proxy cannot verify the details; unavailable confirmation may delay collection.

Needs: paper tickets, a visible inspection surface and staff practice asking a neutral question. Daily check-ins review disputed pickups and revisions. This assumes customers can recognize important features. It is weaker for hidden construction details, customers who agree automatically, and collections by uninformed proxies.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, alternate comparable pickup blocks between this customer check and the usual handoff, preserving traceable revisions in both. Count orders, pre-release discrepancies, wrong handoffs reported afterward, added pickup seconds, and correction minutes and remakes. Ask about unresolved pickups at each daily check-in. Before launch, role-play a swapped item and a proxy who cannot describe the order; release without detection or escalation falsifies the procedure. Compare mismatch and burden rates with the simpler handoff. Separate customer-preference changes from failures to meet the recorded order; limited follow-up means some released errors may remain unreported.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One accountable owner from intake through collection
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce information loss by assigning one worker responsibility for each order from intake through release. The owner records and confirms the customer's requirements, performs or coordinates production, handles the permitted revision, and prepares the order for collection. Questions return to that person instead of passing through several informal summaries. Ownership changes require an explicit transfer; placing a ticket on another worker's bench does not transfer responsibility.

Use existing paper tickets with a unique order number, customer identifier, specification, promised time and owner's initials. Distribute new orders among the four workers according to current workload. At the two daily check-ins, identify orders due before their owner leaves and transfer responsibility where necessary. The receiving owner reads the ticket, inspects the work in progress and initials a dated transfer entry. Preserve earlier entries.

Record the customer's one allowed change as a dated R1 addition attached to the original ticket. Retain the original wording and mark which instructions R1 replaces. Whoever receives the change records it immediately; production pauses until the owner acknowledges it and checks whether existing work needs correction. Promise changes explicitly to the customer.

Failure path: if the owner is unavailable or instructions conflict, the order waits for an explicit ownership transfer or documented clarification. Another worker can continue taking same-day orders and quote feasible completion times. Before departure, each owner must name a successor for outstanding work.

Needs: ticket space for ownership and transfer entries, a brief staff walkthrough and workload review during existing check-ins. This assumes workers can handle a substantial portion of an order or coordinate specialist work. It may reduce forgotten changes and ambiguous responsibility, but cannot reliably detect an owner's own fabrication error. Uneven workloads and owner absences are the main practical limits.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, alternate comparable half-day intake blocks between accountable ownership and usual shared handling, keeping visible revision histories in both. Follow each order through collection. Record released mismatches, discrepancies caught earlier, added intake/transfer/pickup staff-seconds, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. Also count transfers and overdue orders. Before launch, simulate a revision received while the owner is absent: work continuing without acknowledgment or explicit transfer exposes a failure. Compare mismatch rates and burden per order; small counts and differences in order complexity limit conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Physically isolated order workspaces
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent accidental mixing by giving each active order an exclusive, visibly bounded space. Components, work in progress, finished goods and the paper ticket remain together inside that space. Each worker has only one order open on their immediate work surface at a time. Before switching, they return every component to its order's space and clear the surface. This changes the physical opportunity for a swap, rather than adding another final inspection.

Use folded paper tickets as boundary markers on existing shelves or benches. Mark each space and ticket with the same unique order number; record the customer identifier, specification and promised time on the ticket. Several orders may be accepted and queued, including same-day orders, but production starts only when an adequate separate space is available. Bulky items need their own clearly bounded bench or floor position. Shared tools can move between orders; order-specific parts cannot be left in a common loose pile.

Preserve the single allowed customer change on a dated R1 slip attached to the original instructions. Mark the affected space 'revision pending' and stop work there until the maker acknowledges R1. Separate superseded components within that space and label them 'do not use'; retain the earlier instructions legibly. The two daily check-ins reconcile occupied spaces, pending revisions and orders approaching their promised times.

Failure path: loose components with uncertain ownership, two orders found in one space, or insufficient room trigger a hold on the affected work. Reconstruct ownership from tickets and customer clarification before proceeding. Continue taking orders with feasible promised times; never create an unmarked overflow pile.

Needs: existing paper, pens, usable work surfaces and consistent clearing between jobs. This assumes the shop has enough space for its typical workload. It is strongest where similar components get mixed and weaker where mistakes originate in misunderstood specifications or hidden workmanship.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate comparable production blocks between isolated spaces and current staging, preserving revision history in both. Keep each order under its assigned method through completion. Record released mismatches, mixed or unidentified parts caught internally, added sorting/setup/pickup staff-seconds, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. Record space-related delays as well. Before launch, use mock components to test an interrupted job switch and a revision leaving an obsolete part: either part entering another order or returning to production undetected falsifies the isolation rule. Compare rates per completed order, noting workload and available-space differences; few errors leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Translate requests into a fixed production recipe
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce errors before production by translating each customer's conversational request into a short, consistently ordered production recipe. Instead of relying on free-text descriptions such as 'the usual blue one, slightly bigger,' every ticket specifies item type, quantity, size with units, material, color, exact personalization and any orientation or placement. Staff explicitly mark irrelevant fields. Establish shared terms for the shop's common options during an existing check-in; unusual requests remain acceptable but require a precise description or customer-approved sketch.

Confirm the translated recipe with the customer at the counter or by phone readback. The maker follows the fields in their printed or handwritten order and marks each completed step. Give the ticket and finished item the same unique order number; at pickup, record the releasing worker's initials and compare the item with the recipe. The distinctive intervention is removing ambiguous translation between intake and making; identification at release supplies basic traceability.

For the permitted change, retain the original recipe and attach a dated R1 ticket containing the complete revised recipe. Identify changed fields and mark the original superseded without obscuring it. Production pauses until the maker acknowledges R1; any completed steps affected by the change must be reconsidered.

Failure path: an undefined term, missing required field, conflicting versions or customization that cannot be expressed clearly puts the affected order on hold for clarification. Record the resolution and tell the customer about any timing impact. Continue accepting same-day orders with feasible promised times.

Needs: existing tickets, pens and a handwritten field guide, agreed within the two daily check-ins. This assumes ambiguous specifications contribute materially to errors and that common products have describable attributes. It offers less protection against selecting another customer's correctly made item, and an incorrect shared definition could propagate mistakes.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, alternate comparable intake blocks between structured recipes and free-text tickets, retaining identical numbering, revision history and pickup checks in both. Follow orders through collection. Record mismatches caught before release and reported afterward per collected order, added intake and handoff staff-seconds, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. Review unresolved cases at both daily check-ins. Before launch, have two workers independently interpret several ambiguous mock requests under each format, including one revision. If structured recipes still yield different intended products, revise or reject the field definitions. Reduced interpretation disagreement would support the mechanism but would not establish fewer wrong handoffs; low order counts or unreported errors leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: One accountable owner per order
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce information loss by assigning one worker responsibility for each order from intake through preparation and pickup. Instead of allowing any available worker to advance an unfamiliar order, the named owner handles its decisions and normally retrieves the finished item. Other staff can perform specified tasks, but questions and completion reports return to that owner. This could reduce mistakes caused by several workers each assuming someone else understood the customization.

At intake, record an order number, customer identifier, specification, promised time and owner on an existing paper ticket. Confirm the specification with the customer. Allocate new orders among the four workers according to current workload; ownership does not require extra staffing. At the two daily check-ins, owners identify orders due before their next absence and explicitly transfer responsibility where necessary. The receiving owner writes their name and the transfer time; the previous name remains legible.

For the customer's one permitted change, attach a dated R1 ticket describing the change and retain the original instructions. The owner records whether work has started and acknowledges the revision before proceeding. Responsibility transfers must include both versions.

Failure path: if the owner is unavailable, a named replacement reviews the complete record and accepts responsibility before advancing or releasing the order. Ambiguous specifications or uncertain revision status put that order on hold while staff contact the customer. New same-day orders continue to be accepted, with feasible promised times.

Needs: existing tickets, pens and brief workload allocation at the existing check-ins. This assumes owners can remain sufficiently involved across the order's duration. Frequent absences or excessive workload may erase the benefit. Ownership alone cannot detect every manufacturing error and may concentrate delays around one busy worker.
EXPAND.experiment: For two weeks, alternate comparable half-days between named ownership and ordinary shared responsibility, retaining revision history in both. Record order counts, staff transfers, pre-release mismatches, reported wrong releases, added intake and pickup seconds, waiting time, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. Before starting, simulate an owner leaving with an unfinished revised order: a replacement proceeding without accepting the complete record falsifies the transfer procedure. Compare mismatch rates and burden per order; examine whether delays cluster around particular owners. A small number of orders or errors will leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Separate each order physically throughout production
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent components and finished pieces from becoming mixed by giving each active order an exclusive physical space. The intervention changes where objects can be placed, reducing opportunities for a correct item to migrate into another customer's order. It does not depend primarily on adding another inspection.

Use existing clear shelf sections or counter spaces, divided by folded paper markers. Assign each space an order number and keep that order's ticket, components and finished pieces together. Only one order may occupy a space. At shared equipment, bring forward one order's components at a time and return them to their assigned space before fetching another order. For multi-piece orders, record the expected quantity on the space marker so partial sets remain visibly incomplete. Staff retrieve an entire completed set from its space for collection.

At intake, confirm and record the customer identifier, specification and promised time. Preserve the original ticket when the customer uses their one change: attach a dated R1 slip and have the maker acknowledge it. Remove superseded components from the active space and place them separately with an explicit 'obsolete—do not use' paper label linked to the order. Retain the written history.

Failure path: an unassigned item, mixed space or missing component stops progress on the affected orders. Staff reconstruct their contents from the tickets and document the resolution before continuing. If every space is occupied, accept further same-day orders on paper and queue their production until a space becomes available, quoting feasible times.

Needs: sufficient existing surface or shelf space, paper markers and discipline at shared equipment. Use the daily check-ins to resolve orphaned pieces and queued orders. This works best for portable, separable items. Oversized goods, tiny indistinguishable components or insufficient space may make it impractical. It will not prevent an accurately segregated item from being made to the wrong specification.
EXPAND.experiment: Over two weeks, alternate comparable half-days between exclusive order spaces and the usual placement method, with retained revisions in both. Track order volume, mixed or orphaned components, mismatches caught, wrong releases, added handling and pickup seconds, queue delays, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. First stage two similar orders sharing equipment, including one revision that makes a component obsolete. Mixing components or returning the obsolete piece to active work falsifies the containment rule. Compare outcomes with ordinary placement and inspect whether space shortages create unacceptable delays. No observed mix-ups in a small sample does not establish effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Explicit recovery after interruptions
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent workers from resuming the wrong order or continuing from an outdated instruction after a phone call, counter request or other interruption. The design externalizes the worker's place in the task, addressing prospective-memory failures that can occur even when records and labels are correct.

For every order, use an existing paper ticket with its number, customer identifier, confirmed specification and promised time. Before switching away from active work, the worker adds a short pause entry: last completed step, next intended step, and current instruction version. Place the ticket directly with the work. On returning, the worker reads that entry and the current specification before touching the item, then crosses through the pause entry without obscuring it. If an interruption was too abrupt to record a reliable stopping point, mark 'position uncertain' and reconstruct progress before continuing.

Apply the same rule when interrupted during pickup: set the item aside with its ticket, and restart customer-to-order identification when resuming. Continue answering calls and accepting same-day orders; the procedure adds a short recovery action rather than protecting workers through unavailable extra staffing.

Allow the customer's one revision on a dated R1 slip attached to the original ticket. Preserve earlier text. Any pending pause entry becomes invalid when R1 arrives; the maker acknowledges the revision and writes a new next step after assessing work already completed.

Failure path: uncertain progress, contradictory versions or an item separated from its ticket triggers a hold and reconstruction from the record, with customer clarification where necessary. Review unresolved holds and interruption patterns at the two daily check-ins.

Needs: paper, pens and consistent use during busy periods. The assumption is that interruption-related resumption errors contribute materially to mismatches. If most errors originate at intake or item selection without interruption, this mechanism may add effort with little benefit. Entries can also become stale or too vague to help.
EXPAND.experiment: For two weeks, alternate comparable half-days between pause-and-resume entries and ordinary working practice, preserving revision history in both. Tally interrupted orders, pre-release mismatches, reported wrong releases, added recording and recovery seconds, pickup time, and correction staff-minutes and remakes. Before launch, interrupt a practice order, introduce its permitted revision, and ask the worker to resume. Continuing the obsolete next step falsifies the recovery procedure. Compare mismatch and burden rates overall and among interrupted orders. Record rough busy-period workload because interruption frequency may differ between blocks; limited events will leave the causal effect uncertain.

EXPAND.title: A fixed specification grid that exposes missing choices
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent wrong items caused by ambiguous or incomplete intake by replacing free-form descriptions with a small, fixed specification grid on existing paper tickets. The working principle is to expose unresolved choices before production: “usual size,” an empty box or an unexplained abbreviation cannot silently become a maker’s assumption.

At the first staff check-in, identify the attributes that distinguish the shop’s common custom items—for example, base item, size, material, color, wording, quantity and orientation. Draw a reusable example; staff copy the relevant headings onto tickets. Every applicable field must contain an explicit choice; genuinely irrelevant fields get “N/A.” Copy exact customer wording, including capitalization where relevant. Record an order number, customer identifier and promised time. Read the completed choices back on phone orders and show them to counter customers. Unusual work gets an additional labeled field rather than being squeezed into an unsuitable category.

Allow one customer revision through an attached, dated R1 slip showing the affected fields as “was” and “now,” who accepted it, and when. Keep the original ticket legible. The maker initials receipt of R1 and records whether existing work needs alteration or replacement. An unresolved revision blocks work on that order.

Failure path: if a required choice is missing, contradictory or technically infeasible, mark that field unresolved and contact the customer. Continue accepting same-day orders; progress on the affected item resumes after clarification and a feasible completion time is recorded. At both daily check-ins, review unresolved fields and unacknowledged revisions.

Needs are existing tickets, pens, a shared example and a brief staff walkthrough within current shifts. This assumes a manageable set of recurring attributes. It may add little for wholly bespoke work and cannot prevent workers from selecting another customer’s correctly made item. Its value is uncertain until ambiguity is shown to contribute to errors.
EXPAND.experiment: For two weeks, alternate the grid and ordinary free-form tickets across successive orders, assigning the method before hearing the specification. Both methods must retain revision history. Use one paper tally linked to order numbers. Record mismatches detected before release and customer-reported wrong items separately, orders completed, added intake and clarification minutes, and correction burden as staff minutes plus discarded or remade pieces. At each check-in, reconcile tallies with tickets and record whether each discrepancy involved an omitted or ambiguous attribute. Compare mismatch rates per completed order and time per order; report unfinished orders separately. The smallest falsifying check is whether grid tickets still reach production with unresolved choices or produce the same ambiguity-related errors while requiring more service time. A small two-week sample may establish feasibility without establishing a reliable reduction in rare errors.
